author: David Ogilvy
concept: The headline is the decisive element
summary: Ogilvy holds the headline as the most important element of most ads: about five times as many people read the headline as the body, so a headline that fails to sell has wasted most of the spend. He wrote at least sixteen headlines per ad and tested relentlessly.
usable_principle: Spend most of your effort on the opening line/headline; it does the majority of the selling, so generate many candidates and test rather than settling on the first.
sniped_relevance: The opening is where attention is won or lost. A lens for how BJ would lead any piece of communication (a page, a pitch, a post) with a headline that earns the next read. Held as a decision-support + execution-layer lens read against CURRENT_OPERATOR_REALITY_BRIEF: craft BJ can apply to copy, positioning, and offers for whatever he builds, NOT a directive that BJ become a copywriter or run an agency. Does not finalize SNIPED, SNIPED Media, or BASEPLATE direction; photography remains one option among several.

author: David Ogilvy
concept: Advertising builds the long-term brand image
summary: Ogilvy argued every ad is a long-term investment in the brand image, the complex symbol the product accumulates over time; cheap tricks that sell today can erode the symbol that sustains a premium tomorrow.
usable_principle: Treat each piece of communication as a deposit into a durable brand image, not just a short-term response grab; consistency compounds into a premium symbol.
sniped_relevance: Brand as a compounding symbol. A lens for BJ to keep every output consistent with the long-term image he wants, not just the immediate reaction. author: David Ogilvy
concept: Do your homework: research and test everything
summary: Ogilvy's discipline: study the product and the market before writing, and test promises, media, and headlines rather than trusting opinion. He credited research, not flair, for most of his results.
usable_principle: Ground creative work in homework and measurement: test the promise, the channel, and the hook instead of arguing from taste; let evidence settle disputes.
sniped_relevance: Evidence over opinion. A lens for how BJ would validate any offer or message with small tests before scaling, fitting the lean-operator posture. author: David Ogilvy
concept: The promise and the big idea sell, or the ad is ignored
summary: Ogilvy insisted an ad must contain a clear promise/benefit and ideally a big idea; without a compelling promise, even beautiful execution fails to sell. The positioning of what is offered matters more than the polish.
usable_principle: Lead with a sharp, specific promise (what the customer gets) and a single big idea; execution serves the promise, it does not replace it.
sniped_relevance: Promise before polish. A lens for BJ to define the concrete benefit and core idea of any offer before worrying about presentation. author: David Ogilvy
concept: Run the shop: indispensability, standards, and leadership
summary: Confessions opens with how to manage an agency, drawn from Ogilvy's years in a Paris kitchen: make yourself indispensable to clients, inspect every campaign before it ships, set exacting standards, and lead from the front. (Agency-running material, included where it yields an operator principle.)

author: David Ogilvy
concept: Never write an ad you would not want your family to read
summary: Ogilvy's stated rule: never write an advertisement you would not want your own family to read, and do not advertise something you would not let your family use. Honesty is both principle and long-run brand protection.
usable_principle: Hold a personal honesty test for any claim (would I want my family to read/believe this?); deceptive copy wins once and erodes trust thereafter.
sniped_relevance: An ethics test for any message BJ ships: would he stand behind the claim to people he respects? Integrity and long-run trust align. author: Joseph Sugarman
concept: The first sentence has one job: get the second read
summary: Sugarman's core mechanic: every element of an ad (headline, image, layout) exists only to get the first sentence read, and the first sentence's only purpose is to get the second sentence read, and so on. Make the first sentence short and almost impossible not to finish.
usable_principle: Engineer each line to pull the reader into the next; the first sentence should be so easy and intriguing it is read almost involuntarily.
sniped_relevance: Momentum from the first line. A lens for structuring any BJ writing so the opening compels continued reading rather than front-loading information. author: Joseph Sugarman
concept: The slippery slide: make stopping hard
summary: Sugarman's 'slippery slide': great copy is so engaging the reader slides down it unable to stop, every sentence greasing the way to the next. Friction (confusion, a dull line) breaks the slide and loses the reader.
usable_principle: Remove every point of friction and add pull so the reader cannot comfortably stop; flow is engineered sentence by sentence, not assumed.
sniped_relevance: Engineered flow. A lens for BJ to ruthlessly cut friction and keep momentum in anything meant to be read all the way through. author: Joseph Sugarman
concept: Sell on emotion, justify with logic

author: Gary Halbert
concept: The starving crowd: the market beats the copy
summary: Halbert's most famous lesson: asked what advantage he would want selling hamburgers, the answer is not the best meat or location but a starving crowd. The market (who you sell to, and their hunger) matters more than the copy itself.
usable_principle: Choose the market before the message: a hungry, reachable audience with a real need outperforms brilliant copy aimed at an indifferent one.
sniped_relevance: Demand before craft. A lens for BJ to find a genuinely hungry market for any offer first, rather than perfecting a message no one is waiting for. author: Gary Halbert
concept: Write like a personal letter to one reader
summary: The Boron Letters (written from prison to his son) model copy as a personal, conversational letter to a single reader, plain and direct, hooking from the first impression because you never get a second chance at one.

author: Gary Halbert
